---
title: "peabiru with sf and the tidyverse"
description: >
  From points to maps with the tools you already use: an sf grid, routing
  with the native pipe, dplyr on the tibbles peabiru returns, joins back to
  the geometry and ggplot2's geom_sf().
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
source("setup.R")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 6, dpi = 110, out.width = "100%")
```

peabiru returns tibbles, and `sf` tibbles where the result has a geometry,
so its results go straight into 'dplyr' and 'ggplot2'. This article walks
from a set of points to maps of travel times, accessibility, isochrones and
trips, on the São Paulo sample network shipped with the package (the streets
around Avenida Paulista and the SPTrans GTFS feed), so that it runs offline
in a few seconds.

```{r packages, message = FALSE}
library(peabiru)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

data_path <- system.file("extdata/spo", package = "peabiru")
network <- build_network(data_path, n_threads = 2)
departure <- as.POSIXct("2019-05-13 14:00:00", tz = "America/Sao_Paulo")
```

## Points and a grid as sf

The sample has 27 points with their population and the jobs, schools and
health care in each. As an `sf` tibble they keep those columns next to the
geometry:

```{r points}
points <- read.csv(file.path(data_path, "spo_points.csv")) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)
points
```

A hexagonal grid over the network gives the areas to map. Grids are drawn in
metres, so this one is made in SIRGAS 2000 / UTM zone 23S (EPSG:31983), the
projected system of São Paulo, and kept there: peabiru takes `sf` points in
any coordinate reference system and reprojects them to WGS 84 itself.

```{r grid}
area <- street_network_bbox(network) |> st_transform(31983)
hexagons <- st_make_grid(area, cellsize = 300, square = FALSE) |>
  st_as_sf() |>
  st_set_geometry("geometry") |>
  mutate(id = sprintf("h%03d", row_number()), .before = 1)
# the attributes (the id) hold for the whole hexagon, so for its centre too
centres <- hexagons |> st_set_agr("constant") |> st_centroid()
nrow(hexagons)
```

## A travel-time matrix with the pipe

The network is the first argument of every routing function, so a call reads
from left to right with the native pipe. From the centre of every hexagon to
the 27 points, walking and by public transport:

```{r ttm}
ttm <- network |>
  travel_time_matrix(origins = centres, destinations = points,
                     mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"), departure_datetime = departure,
                     max_trip_duration = 60, seed = 42, n_threads = 2)
ttm
```

The centres are in UTM, so peabiru says it reprojected them (the points were
already in WGS 84). The message has its own class, `peabiru_reprojected`;
`suppressMessages()` silences it.

## dplyr on the result

The result is a tibble with one row per pair, ready for dplyr verbs. For each
hexagon, the median time to the 27 points and how many of them are within
20 minutes:

```{r summary}
by_hexagon <- ttm |>
  group_by(id = from_id) |>
  summarise(median_time = median(travel_time_p50),
            within_20 = sum(travel_time_p50 <= 20),
            .groups = "drop")
by_hexagon |> arrange(median_time)
```

## Back to the geometry

To map the summary, join it to the hexagons. **Put the `sf` object on the
left**: `left_join()` keeps the class of its first argument, so
`hexagons |> left_join(by_hexagon)` is an `sf` with the new columns, while
`by_hexagon |> left_join(hexagons)` is a plain tibble that carries the
geometry as a column without being `sf` (`st_as_sf()` would turn it back).

```{r join}
mapped <- hexagons |> left_join(by_hexagon, by = "id")
class(mapped)
class(by_hexagon |> left_join(hexagons, by = "id"))
```

A hexagon whose centre reached none of the points within the hour would
have no row in the matrix; the join would leave it `NA`, and `geom_sf()`
would draw it grey.

```{r median-map, fig.alt = "A map of hexagons over central São Paulo, with the main streets, coloured by the median travel time walking and by public transport from each hexagon to the 27 sample points: about 15 minutes in the middle and to the west, where the points are, rising to about 50 minutes at the eastern edge."}
streets <- street_network_to_sf(network)$edges |>
  filter(street_class %in% c("PRIMARY", "SECONDARY"))

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = mapped, aes(fill = median_time), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = streets, colour = "#4a5a5f", linewidth = 0.25, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#7a3318", high = "#f5d3b6", na.value = "grey85",
                      name = "Median\nminutes") +
  theme_void()
```

## Accessibility as a choropleth

`accessibility()` counts, for each origin, the opportunities within the
cutoff. The destinations carry the opportunity columns; the origins are the
hexagon centres again:

```{r access}
jobs <- network |>
  accessibility(origins = centres, destinations = points,
                opportunities_colnames = c("jobs", "schools"),
                mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"), departure_datetime = departure,
                cutoffs = c(15, 30), seed = 42, n_threads = 2) |>
  suppressMessages()
jobs |>
  group_by(opportunity, cutoff) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(accessibility), max = max(accessibility), .groups = "drop")
```

One cutoff and one opportunity per map, or `facet_wrap()` over the two
cutoffs after the join:

```{r access-map, fig.height = 4.4, fig.alt = "Two maps of hexagons, for 15 and 30 minutes, coloured by the number of jobs reachable walking and by public transport: within 15 minutes a few hexagons west of the centre reach more than 50 thousand jobs; within 30 minutes most of the western two thirds reach about 100 thousand, and the eastern edge few."}
hexagons |>
  inner_join(filter(jobs, opportunity == "jobs"), by = "id") |>
  mutate(cutoff = paste(cutoff, "minutes")) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = accessibility / 1000), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#e8efe9", high = "#2f6b4f", name = "Jobs\n(thousands)") +
  facet_wrap(~cutoff) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0))
```

`inner_join()` keeps only the hexagons with a value, and the result is still
`sf`, because the `sf` object is on the left.

## Isochrones and itineraries as layers

`isochrone()`, `detailed_itineraries()` and `trip_options()` return `sf`
tibbles in WGS 84 that `geom_sf()` draws as they are. ggplot2 puts every layer
in the coordinate system of the first, so the UTM hexagons and the WGS 84
results share one map.

```{r layers}
origin <- points |> filter(id == "89a8100c037ffff")
destination <- points |> filter(id == "89a8100c39bffff")

reach <- network |>
  isochrone(origins = origin, mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"), cutoffs = c(0, 10, 20, 30),
            departure_datetime = departure, seed = 42, n_threads = 2)
reach

cycling <- network |>
  detailed_itineraries(origins = origin, destinations = destination, mode = "BICYCLE",
                       departure_datetime = departure, n_threads = 2)
cycling |> select(mode, segment_duration, distance)
```

The bundled feed is frequency-based, so `detailed_itineraries()` routes
street modes only (as r5r does); the public transport trip comes from
`trip_options()` below.

## trip_options() with dplyr

`trip_options()` returns a list of tables: `options` (one row per trip worth
considering), `itineraries` (an `sf` of their legs) and, with
`by_departure = TRUE`, `departures`. Its options for the same pair:

```{r options}
trips <- network |>
  trip_options(origins = origin, destinations = destination,
               departure_datetime = departure, n_threads = 2)
trips$options |> select(option, total_time, transfers, walk_time, description)
```

The legs summarise with dplyr like any table; `st_drop_geometry()` first
when the lines are not needed, which keeps the summary light:

```{r legs}
trips$itineraries |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  group_by(option) |>
  summarise(legs = n(), riding = sum(segment_duration[mode != "WALK"]),
            walking = sum(segment_duration[mode == "WALK"]), metres = sum(distance))
```

On one map: the isochrones, the cycling route and the fastest public
transport option, its legs coloured by mode.

```{r layers-map, fig.height = 7.2, fig.alt = "A map over the hexagon grid with three nested areas reached from one point within 10, 20 and 30 minutes walking and by public transport, the dashed cycling route to a point about two kilometres to the north-east, and the fastest public transport option to it: a walk, a metro ride and another walk."}
fastest <- trips$itineraries |> filter(option == 1)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = hexagons, fill = NA, colour = "grey80", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = reach |> arrange(desc(isochrone)), aes(fill = factor(isochrone)),
          colour = NA, alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_sf(data = cycling, colour = "#4a5a5f", linewidth = 0.9, linetype = "22") +
  geom_sf(data = fastest, aes(colour = mode), linewidth = 1.4) +
  geom_sf(data = bind_rows(origin, destination), size = 2.5, shape = 21,
          fill = "white", colour = "black") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`10` = "#a2502a", `20` = "#d46f3d", `30` = "#f5d3b6"),
                    name = "Within\n(minutes)") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(WALK = "#c98a1d", SUBWAY = "#2f6b4f", BUS = "#2f6b4f",
                                 RAIL = "#2f6b4f"),
                      name = "Fastest by\npublic transport") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical",
        plot.margin = margin(5, 5, 12, 5))
```

## Choosing the class of the results

Every function returns tibbles because `options(peabiru.output = )` is
`"tibble"` by default. It is read at each call; set it once at the top of a
script:

- `"data.frame"` gives base data frames (and plain `sf`), for code written
  for them;
- `"data.table"` gives `data.table`s, exactly as r5r returns them (`sf`
  `data.table`s for isochrones and itineraries): the better choice for large
  matrices, where data.table's grouping by reference saves time and memory,
  and for scripts written for r5r.

```{r data-table, message = FALSE, eval = requireNamespace("data.table", quietly = TRUE)}
library(data.table)
options(peabiru.output = "data.table")
ttm_dt <- network |>
  travel_time_matrix(origins = centres, destinations = points,
                     mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"), departure_datetime = departure,
                     max_trip_duration = 60, seed = 42, n_threads = 2) |>
  suppressMessages()
class(ttm_dt)
ttm_dt[, .(median_time = median(travel_time_p50)), by = .(id = from_id)][order(median_time)][1:3]
options(peabiru.output = NULL) # back to the default, tibbles
```

The rows, columns, types and values are the same whatever the class: for a
table without geometry, `as.data.frame()` of any of the three gives the same
data frame.
